claims.text: Short-range chemical ordering primarily governs hardness and strength in single-phase high-entropy alloys.
Short-range chemical ordering increases lattice friction and alters dislocation pathways.
Higher levels of short-range ordering produce greater strengthening through augmented defect interactions.
Nominally equiatomic CrCoNi is an appropriate single-phase FCC model alloy for the proposed comparison.
The initial CrCoNi alloy can have minimal pre-existing short-range ordering.
Changing thermal treatment can alter the type or degree of short-range chemical ordering in CrCoNi or NiCoCr.
Electron nanodiffraction, atom-probe tomography, scattering, and atomistic simulations can be combined to characterize short-range ordering.
Samples with different annealing histories should be mechanically tested under identical strain-rate and environmental conditions.
The measured degree of local chemical ordering is the structural mediator linking annealing to mechanical response.
Short-range ordering changes stacking-fault or generalized planar-fault energies and promotes diffuse antiphase-boundary development.
Short-range ordering creates a more heterogeneous or rugged local energy landscape that raises activation barriers for dislocation motion.
Increasing short-range order within a stable single-phase regime will increase hardness and yield strength relative to a near-random baseline.
The largest strength increases will occur when substantial short-range order develops without secondary-phase formation.
A sufficiently high-temperature or sufficiently short anneal can provide a comparatively near-random baseline.
The hypothesis is restricted to predominantly single-phase FCC alloys and treatments for which second-phase formation is negligible.
Extremely high temperatures or prolonged annealing can introduce additional phases or excessive grain growth.
Composition, processing, microstructure, and grain orientation can complicate the relationship between short-range order and mechanical response.

Failure to observe a consistent relationship between measured short-range order and both hardness and yield strength across annealing conditions would falsify the claim that short-range order is dominant.
